name: Neck tension / platysma flex
lead: Neck tension or platysma flexing is a posing practice in which a person deliberately contracts the platysma, the thin superficial muscle of the front of the neck, to make the jaw-neck transition and lower jawline look more defined, mostly for photographs or mirror checks. The intended payoff is a sharper line under the chin and a tighter-looking neck for the length of the pose.

The platysma is a broad, thin sheet lying just beneath the subcutaneous fat and overlapping the sternocleidomastoid. When it contracts it slightly wrinkles the neck skin and produces a 'bowstring' effect, and its front portion can pull the lower lip and mouth corners down.[1] Because it sits directly under the skin, its contraction changes the visible contour of the neck.[1]

Visible platysmal bands (platysma dyskinesia, sometimes called 'turkey neck') tend to appear with age and can be aggravated by weightlifting and facelifts, according to Wikipedia.[1] Clinical research on the platysma has focused on those bands and their treatment with botulinum toxin; no published clinical study has tested voluntary platysma flexing for jawline appearance.

angle.text: While the muscle is tensed, the neck skin pulls taut and the lower face and neck appear more defined in a photo or mirror. The change lasts as long as the contraction does and is used as a posing technique.

infobox: Platysmal bands and botulinum toxin treatment[1][2]

paras: The platysma is supplied by the cervical branch of the facial nerve.[1] Its fibres arise from fascia over the upper chest and shoulder, cross the clavicle and run upward along the neck.[1] Its anterior fibres can depress the lower jaw and pull down the lower lip and corners of the mouth, a smaller role than that of other facial depressor muscles.[1]
Contraction slightly wrinkles the neck skin and produces a bowstring effect.[1] Practitioners of the flex use this tightening to alter the neck's visible outline.

Visible platysmal bands tend to become more prominent with age.[1] Options described in clinical references include conservative management, botulinum toxin injection, platysmaplasty (open or closed) and neck liposuction.[1] These are separate from voluntary flexing as practised online.

A 2019 systematic review in the Aesthetic Surgery Journal by Sugrue, Kelly and McInerney covered three studies with 78 patients who received botulinum toxin for mild to moderate platysma bands.[2] Using the Merz platysma score, improvement appeared at about two weeks and persisted at three months, complications were reported in 15.4 percent of patients and none required further intervention.[2] The authors concluded that botulinum toxin is highly effective for isolated platysma bands.[2]

No specific harms of voluntary flexing have been documented. Wikipedia notes weightlifting can aggravate platysmal bands.[1] In the botulinum toxin review, the complications included bruising, mild difficulty swallowing and neck weakness.[2]
No studies found on platysma flexing or neck exercises for jawline appearance. Related clinical research concerns botulinum toxin treatment of platysma bands, summarized above.[2]

card.summary: Tensing the neck muscle for a sharper jaw-neck line in photos; a posing habit with no studies behind it.
card.note: Temporary visual effect only while flexed; no trials exist.

quick.overview:
Platysma flexing means deliberately tightening the thin muscle across the front of the neck so the area under the jaw looks more defined, usually for a photo.

It is discussed as a posing technique rather than a lasting change. No published studies have examined it.
quick.mechanism: The platysma sits just under the skin of the neck; contracting it tightens and wrinkles the overlying skin and can pull the lower lip and mouth corners downward [1].
quick.risks: No specific harms have been documented for the practice. Clinical sources note that prominent platysmal bands can be aggravated by some activities such as weightlifting [1]. No trials exist.
